Reversible Migration

7 September 2022 · Bodil Hald

A migration is reversible when the system can run correctly on either side of it for as long as you need. That is a stronger property than having written a down script, and it is the one that decides whether a release can be rolled back on a Friday evening without a meeting.

The usual failure is a migration that is reversible in the database and not in the code. The column is dropped in one deploy and the code that read it in the next, so for the window between them the running system is one version away from a crash in either direction. Nothing about the down script tells you that.

The four shapes

ChangeReversible?Why
Add a nullable columnYesOld code ignores it.
Add a NOT NULL columnNoOld inserts have no value for it.
Rename a columnNoNeither version can read both names.
Add then backfill then enforceYesEach step runs on both.

The last row is the technique, and it is the whole of the technique. Every irreversible change decomposes into a sequence of reversible ones, at the price of more deploys. Teams that find this tedious are measuring the cost of the deploys and not the cost of the rollback they will eventually want.

When to stop bothering

Reversibility is insurance, and insurance has a premium. For a table nothing depends on, in a system with one deployable and one operator, the premium is larger than the risk. Say so out loud rather than letting the practice quietly lapse, because a practice that lapses silently comes back as a surprise.

The judgement is about blast radius, not about size. A two-line migration on the table every request reads deserves the full sequence; a thousand-line one on a reporting table that is rebuilt nightly does not.
